title: Být & mít (to be / to have)
blurb: Master Czech's two most essential verbs — to be and to have — in every person.

vocab.translation: to be — I am, you are, he/she/it is
vocab.example: Jsem z Indie a ty jsi odkud?

vocab.translation: to be — we are, you are (pl./formal), they are
vocab.example: Jsme unavení, ale vy jste v pořádku?

vocab.translation: to have — I have, you have, he/she/it has
vocab.example: Mám bratra, a ty máš sourozence?

vocab.translation: to have — we have, you have (pl./formal), they have
vocab.example: Máme byt v Praze, a oni mají dům.

vocab.translation: I am not, I don't have

vocab.example: Praha je hlavní město. Londýn není v Česku.

grammarNote.title: Ne- glues straight onto the verb
grammarNote.text: Být and mít are two of the few Czech verbs you must simply memorize as full paradigms — jsem/jsi/je/jsme/jste/jsou and mám/máš/má/máme/máte/mají don't follow the regular -it/-at/-et conjugation patterns you'll meet later. Negation is even simpler than in English: instead of adding a helper word like "don't", Czech just glues ne- onto the front of the verb — jsem → nejsem, mám → nemám. There's no separate negative auxiliary to learn.

check.prompt: How do you say "I have" in Czech?
check.explanation: „Mám“ is the first-person singular of mít (to have). „Jsem“ is "I am" (from být).
check.note: Mixing up jsem and mám is the most common beginner error with these two verbs — both are irregular and both come up constantly.
The -me ending across Czech verbs consistently marks "we" — a pattern that repeats far beyond just být.

check.prompt: Fill in the correct form of být: On ___ doktor. (He is a doctor.)
check.explanation: „Je“ is the third-person singular (on/ona/ono) form of být.
check.note: „Je“ is one of the most common words in Czech — it's also used impersonally, e.g. „Je zima“ (It's cold).

check.explanation: Negate mít by adding ne- directly to the verb: mám → nemám.
check.note: This ne- + verb pattern works the same way for every Czech verb, not just mít and být.

title: Basic word order & questions
blurb: Ask questions naturally: question words, yes/no questions, and how Czech word order really works.

grammarNote.title: No "do" in questions — just intonation
grammarNote.text: English needs a helper verb to ask a yes/no question ("Do you have time?"). Czech doesn't — you ask the exact same sentence you'd use to state a fact, just with rising intonation in speech or a question mark in writing: Máš čas. (You have time.) becomes Máš čas? (Do you have time?) with no word added or reordered. For questions with a question word (co, kdo, kde…), that word simply comes first, and the verb usually follows right after it: Kde bydlíš? Because Czech nouns and pronouns carry case endings that show their grammatical role, word order in statements is also more flexible than in English — it shifts to signal emphasis rather than to mark subject vs. object.

check.explanation: „Kde“ means "where". „Kdy“ (very similar-looking) means "when" — a classic mix-up.
check.note: Kde/Kdy differ by one letter and are the single most confused question-word pair for beginners.

check.prompt: Czech forms yes/no questions with a helper word like English "do".
check.explanation: Czech uses no helper verb — the statement word order stays the same and only intonation (or the question mark) signals a question.
check.note: This makes yes/no questions easier than in English once you stop reaching for a Czech "do".

check.explanation: „Jak se jmenuješ?“ literally means "How are you named?" — jak, not co, is used here.
check.note: This is a fixed idiom — Czech asks names with jak, not co, even though English uses "what".

check.prompt: Turn into a question: Bydlíš v Praze. → ___
check.explanation: No word order change is needed — just add a question mark (and rising intonation when speaking).
check.note: Compare this to English, which needs "Do you live in Prague?" — Czech just re-punctuates the same sentence.

title: Nouns & gender (nominative only)
blurb: Spot a noun's grammatical gender from its ending and pair it with ten/ta/to.

grammarNote.title: Guess gender from the ending — then check it with ten/ta/to
grammarNote.text: Every Czech noun has one of three grammatical genders — masculine, feminine, or neuter — shown by the demonstrative you'd pair with it: ten (m.), ta (f.), to (n.). You can usually guess which one from the noun's final letter: nouns ending in a consonant are typically masculine (muž, stůl), nouns ending in -a or -e/-ě are typically feminine (žena, kniha), and nouns ending in -o or -í/-e are typically neuter (auto, město). This isn't just trivia — gender determines which endings adjectives, pronouns, and later case forms have to take, so getting comfortable spotting it now pays off in every lesson from here on.

check.prompt: Which demonstrative goes with the neuter noun „auto“?
check.explanation: „To auto“ — auto ends in -o, a typical neuter ending, so it pairs with to.
check.note: Ty is plural ("these/those") and doesn't apply to a single noun like auto.

check.prompt: Nouns ending in a consonant are usually masculine.
check.explanation: This is the most reliable of the three patterns — muž, stůl, dům, byt all end in a consonant and are all masculine.
check.note: It's a strong pattern, not an absolute rule — a handful of feminine nouns like „tramvaj“ also end in a consonant.

check.explanation: Kniha ends in -a, a typical feminine ending, so it takes ta.
check.note: Once you know a noun's gender, the right demonstrative becomes automatic — -a instantly signals ta.

check.prompt: „ten muž“ is masculine. Give the matching feminine phrase for "woman": „___ žena“
check.explanation: Žena ends in -a, so it pairs with the feminine demonstrative ta.
check.note: This same ten/ta/to swap is the fastest way to double-check a noun's gender before you speak.
